explanations.explanation: Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown Elizabeth, the baby's mother, great mercy, and they rejoiced with her. Nobody stood in the corner with their arms crossed. I think that's how you treat a friend's good news. You show up and you celebrate like it happened to you.

Luke says the opposite. Her neighbors and relatives heard the Lord had shown Elizabeth, the baby's mother, great mercy, and the verse says “…they rejoiced with her.” So the whole neighborhood was on her side. Nobody even tried to rain on this parade.

The text says they were going to name him after his father Zechariah. That was the plan walking in. Zechariah is the baby's dad, and the name was already sitting there like a cookie waiting on a cooling rack. Plans can change fast, though.

Close to the idea of family names, but not what Luke says. The people there were going to name him after his father Zechariah. No grandfather is mentioned in the verse at all. Luke keeps it to the baby's dad.
Luke doesn't mention an uncle anywhere in this scene. He says they were going to name the baby after his father Zechariah. The name on the table was the dad's name. Nobody's uncle gets a vote here.

Elizabeth, the baby's mother, does the opposite. The people were going to name him after his father Zechariah, but she replied, “No! He shall be called John.” That's a short answer with zero wiggle room. She doesn't even say 'let me think about it.'

That's right, she doesn't agree. When they were going to name him Zechariah, his mother Elizabeth replied, “No! He shall be called John.” She starts with a loud “No!” and then gives the name. I'd say she'd made up her mind.
After her “No!” she says, “He shall be called John.” That's it. No speech, no list of options, just the name. And that's the name this baby keeps for the rest of the story.
Samuel was a real name in Israel, and he was a prophet (1 Samuel 3:20). But it isn't the one Elizabeth gives. She says, “He shall be called John.” The name she gives is right there in verse 60.
Jacob, also called Israel (Genesis 32:28), is a famous name, but Elizabeth doesn't pick it. After her “No!” she says, “He shall be called John.” That one name is her whole answer.

explanations.answer: None of her relatives has that name
explanations.explanation: They tell her, “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.” So their objection is about family tradition. They're not saying the name is bad. They're saying nobody in the family has it. I think Elizabeth is about to show them that family tradition isn't the only thing in the room.

explanations.answer: The priests already picked a name
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't say anything about priests picking a name. The people there say, “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.” Their point is about the family. Nobody mentions a committee.

explanations.answer: Only a king could use that name
explanations.explanation: No king comes up in this scene. Their pushback is about her family: “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.” That's the whole objection. It's about relatives, not royalty.

Zechariah asks for a tablet and writes his answer. He can't speak, so writing is how he gets it across. I spent a lot of time unable to say a word in the back of a drawer, so I'd have loved one of those. It's a little slower than talking, but it gets the job done.
Nobody asks for a lamp here. Luke says Zechariah asked for a tablet and wrote on it. A lamp can light up a room, but it can't spell out a name. He needed something to write on.
A staff is good for walking, but Zechariah isn't going anywhere. Luke says he asked for a tablet, and then he wrote his answer on it. You can't write a name with a walking stick, at least not neatly.

He writes, “His name is John.” That's the same name Elizabeth already gave. And Luke says they were all amazed. The mom said it out loud, the dad wrote it down, and the room had nothing left to argue about.
It's actually the same name. Elizabeth says, “He shall be called John,” and Zechariah writes, “His name is John.” Luke says they were all amazed. Mom and Dad land on the very same name.

Immediately his mouth is opened and his tongue is released, and he begins to speak, praising God. Think about that. After all that silence, the first thing out of his mouth is praise. I think that tells you where his heart was.
Luke doesn't say he questions anybody. When his tongue is released, he begins to speak, praising God. The relatives had done plenty of questioning already. Zechariah's first words go to God.
The neighbors are standing right there, but they aren't who he speaks to first. Luke says he began to speak, praising God. His words go up before they go sideways.

All who heard this wondered in their hearts and asked, “What then will this child become?” They can tell something unusual is going on. And Luke adds that the Lord's hand was with him. The people are curious and the text gives them a reason to be.

explanations.answer: Where did this child come from
explanations.explanation: That's a fair question, but it isn't the one Luke gives. The people ask, “What then will this child become?” They're looking ahead, not back. Their wondering is about his future.

The name was the big talk in the room, so I see why you'd pick this one. But Luke says they asked, “What then will this child become?” Their wondering moves from the name to the child's future. They're thinking bigger than the name.
Luke says it plainly: “For the Lord's hand was with him.” That's what he says right after people ask what this child will become. The text gives that as a fact about John. Nobody had to guess.

Luke says the opposite. Right after the people ask, “What then will this child become?” he adds, “For the Lord's hand was with him.” So the people aren't wondering about a baby with nothing special going on.

explanations.answer: He has visited and redeemed His people
explanations.explanation: Zechariah, the baby's father, says, “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and redeemed His people.” That's his reason for the blessing. I can relate. When someone has come and gotten you out of the dark, praise comes easy.

explanations.answer: He has given a new law to His people
explanations.explanation: That's not what Zechariah says. After “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,” his reason is “because He has visited and redeemed His people.” He talks about God coming to His people, not about handing them anything new to follow.

explanations.answer: He has sent rain on the land of His people
explanations.explanation: Rain would be good news, but it isn't Zechariah's reason. He says, “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and redeemed His people.” His blessing is about God visiting and redeeming. The weather doesn't come up.

Zechariah says, “He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David.” David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3). So Zechariah ties this salvation to David's house. That's a big hint about where it's coming from.

Moses was the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), so I see the pull. But Zechariah says the horn of salvation is raised up “in the house of His servant David.” David is the name in the verse.

Aaron was Israel's first priest (Exodus 28:1), and Zechariah himself is a priest's name-sake kind of guy, so I get it. But the verse says the horn of salvation is raised up “in the house of His servant David.” The house here is David's.

Zechariah says the opposite. He says God raised up this salvation “as He spoke through His holy prophets, those of ages past.” So the prophets had already spoken about it. This didn't come out of nowhere.

That's right. Zechariah says God raised up this salvation “as He spoke through His holy prophets, those of ages past.” The prophets spoke of it long before. What's happening now is what they said was coming.
Zechariah says it's “the oath He swore to our father Abraham.” Abraham is the man he calls the father of his people. So God's holy covenant goes way back, and Zechariah says God remembers it.
Joseph was one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 37:2), but he isn't the one Zechariah names. He says the oath is the one God swore “to our father Abraham.” Abraham is the name in verse 73.
Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36), and a famous one. But Zechariah isn't talking about him here. He says God swore the oath “to our father Abraham.” That's the name in the verse.

Zechariah says God grants deliverance from hostile hands, “that we may serve Him without fear.” That's a big deal for people who've been under pressure. Serving Him without fear means doing it with no dread hanging over them.
Zechariah doesn't say anything like that. He says deliverance from hostile hands comes “that we may serve Him without fear.” The word is fear, not temple. Nothing in his words takes the temple away.

No, Zechariah doesn't say that. He's talking about deliverance from hostile hands, “that we may serve Him without fear.” And remember, he just spoke of a horn of salvation in the house of David, who was a king. So he isn't pushing kings out.

Zechariah says they will serve Him “in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives.” Notice how long that lasts. It's all the days of their lives, not just on the good ones. That's a long stretch of faithful serving.
It's actually true. Zechariah says they'll serve Him “in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives.” He doesn't narrow it to a season or a special day. He says all their days.

Zechariah tells his son, “you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him.” John's part is to go first and get the way ready. He doesn't take over the main event. I think there's a lot of honor in that kind of job.
Zechariah doesn't give John a battle job. He says John “will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him.” Preparing the way is the job. Swords don't come up.

Building a house isn't part of John's assignment here. Zechariah says John will go before the Lord “to prepare the way for Him.” John gets the road ready, not a building. Hammers can stay in the toolbox.

Zechariah says John will give God's people “the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins.” So the knowledge and the forgiveness go together in his words. That's the message John carries.

Zechariah does tie them together. He says John will give God's people “the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins.” Forgiveness of sins is right there in the verse. It's the heart of the message.

Zechariah says the Dawn will visit “to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death.” I know a little about dark places, and light means a lot when you've been in one. That's who the light is for.
Comfort isn't what Zechariah mentions. He says the Dawn will come “to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death.” The light is for people sitting in the dark.

explanations.answer: Those who live by the sea
explanations.explanation: No seaside in this verse. Zechariah says the Dawn will come “to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death.” The people he names are the ones in the dark, wherever they live.

Luke says John “lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel.” He grows up and becomes strong in spirit out there. So his quiet years happen away from the crowds. Then the time comes for him to appear to Israel.
Luke doesn't put John in a city. He says the child “lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel.” His growing up happens out away from the busy places.
Luke doesn't say village. He says John “lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel.” The wilderness is where he waits for that day.
